1	% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)
2	
3	\section{Introduction}
4	\label{sec:introduction}
5	
6	Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
7	We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
8	Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
9	At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.
10	
11	Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
12	Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
13	Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
14	Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
15	Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.
16	
17	We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
18	A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) under both zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned settings, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework grounded in the observation that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

5	\section{Method}
6	\label{sec:method}
7	
8	\input{fig1_framework}
9	
10	We present OntoCoDec, a framework that translates IE ontologies into token-level constraints enforced during autoregressive generation.
11	The design is guided by a decidability analysis of IE type constraints.
12	
13	\paragraph{Constraint decidability taxonomy.}
14	\label{sec:decidability}
15	We classify IE type constraints into three levels: (1)~\emph{context-free}: vocabulary membership and JSON structure; (2)~\emph{prefix-decidable with state}: domain/range type validity, determined at each type-bearing position given the decoded relation type and entity registry; (3)~\emph{non-local}: cross-entity type consistency, which depends on the full output.
16	Unlike code generation where types are statically declared, IE constraints fall into level~2: entity types are inferred from text, the registry is built dynamically, and constraint targets depend on the co-occurring relation.
17	OntoCoDec enforces levels 1--2 (grammar and semantic layers, respectively); level~3 is addressed by beam search or post-hoc resolution (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
18	
19	\smallskip
20	\noindent
21	Existing grammar-constrained decoding frameworks (e.g., XGrammar) enforce level~1 constraints---structural validity and vocabulary membership---but IE domain/range rules require cross-position entity-type state that context-free grammars cannot express.
22	Even when the entity set is finite, encoding type constraints into a DFA requires $O(|\mathcal{E}|^{|\text{entities}|})$ states: for typical SciERC documents (median 17 entities, 6 types), $6^{17} \approx 1.6{\times}10^{13}$ states; for DocRED (median 19 entities, 6 types), $6^{19} \approx 6.1{\times}10^{14}$---well beyond practical construction for online decoding.
23	Formally, domain/range constraints for unbounded entity sets are not context-free (\textbf{Proposition~1}; proof via pumping argument in Appendix~\ref{app:pumping-lemma}): a PDA cannot retrieve the type of entity $e_k$ without destroying stack entries above it.
24	OntoCoDec's semantic layer addresses this with a runtime entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ (a finite map enabling random-access type lookups), avoiding both the theoretical impossibility (unbounded) and the engineering intractability (finite but exponential).
25	
26	\noindent\textbf{Empirical Observation} (scale-dependent enabling dependency)\textbf{.} The grammar layer alone cannot enforce domain/range constraints (Proposition~1), while the semantic layer alone achieves only 24\% DR reduction at 8B without grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}, Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}).
27	The strength of this dependency is scale-dependent: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}), whereas 8B models show only 24\% independent reduction.
28	\smallskip
29	
30	We describe the problem formulation (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), each layer, and two decoding strategies (\S\ref{sec:strategies}); formal analysis of constraint composition is in Section~\ref{sec:composition}.
31	
32	
33	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
34	\label{sec:formulation}
35	
36	\paragraph{IE as structured generation.}
37	Given an input text $x$, a language model generates a structured JSON output $y$:
38	%
39	\begin{equation}\label{eq:output-schema}
40	\resizebox{.88\columnwidth}{!}{$\displaystyle
41	  y = \bigl\{\texttt{entities}: [\{n_i, \tau_i\}],\; \texttt{relations}: [\{h_j, t_j, r_j, \tau^h_j, \tau^t_j\}]\bigr\}
42	$}
43	\end{equation}
44	%
45	where each entity has a name $n_i$ and type $\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$, and each relation specifies head $h_j$, tail $t_j$, relation type $r_j \in \mathcal{R}$, and head/tail entity types $\tau^h_j, \tau^t_j$.
46	The output JSON Schema (\S\ref{sec:grammar}) enforces a fixed field ordering (head $\to$ tail $\to$ relation $\to$ head\_type $\to$ tail\_type) via deterministic grammar compilation, ensuring the relation type $r_j$ is known before entity type fields and enabling sequential domain/range lookups (\S\ref{sec:dynamic-masking}).
47	The grammar structurally enforces entity-before-relation ordering (100\% preservation across all configurations), ensuring the entity registry (\S\ref{sec:entity-registry}) is populated before relation-level type constraints are evaluated; unregistered entities trigger domain-only filtering.
48	
49	\paragraph{Ontology compliance.}
50	Using the ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ defined in \S\ref{sec:background}, we write $\operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau^h : \exists \tau^t,\, (\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)\}$ for domain-valid head types and $\operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h) = \{\tau^t : (\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)\}$ for the conditional range given head type $\tau^h$.
51	Our enforcement target is \emph{pair-based} type validity: $(\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)$ for every triple.
52	The decoder enforces this sequentially: $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$ at head position, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$ at tail position, achieving best-effort pair-based enforcement (pair validity ensured when no fallback is triggered; domain-only filtering otherwise) strictly stronger than independent domain/range checks (which over-permit 33--37\% spurious pairs on SciERC/DocRED; \S\ref{sec:rectangularity}).
53	
54	
55	\subsection{Grammar Layer}
56	\label{sec:grammar}
57	
58	A JSON Schema encoding Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema} with \texttt{enum} constraints ($\mathcal{E}$, $\mathcal{R}$) is compiled into a pushdown automaton via XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}.
59	At step $t$, grammar-valid tokens $G(t) \subseteq V$ pass; all others receive logits $-\infty$, enforcing structural validity, vocabulary membership ($r_j \in \mathcal{R}$, $\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$), but not domain/range constraints (which depend on entity types within each triple).
60	
61	\subsection{Semantic Layer}
62	\label{sec:semantic}
63	
64	The semantic layer enforces domain/range constraints through a stateful logits processor maintaining an entity registry during generation.
65	\emph{Running example}: for \textsc{Used-for} ($\operatorname{dom}{=}\{\textrm{Method}\}$, $\operatorname{range}{=}\{\textrm{Task}\}$), entity ``ResNet'' (Method) passes the head-type check while Material is blocked; ``image classification'' (Task) passes the tail-type check.
66	
67	\paragraph{Entity registry.}
68	\label{sec:entity-registry}
69	The semantic layer builds a registry $\mathcal{D}: \text{name} \to \text{type}$ incrementally during entity generation: each completed entry $\{n_i, \tau_i\}$ adds $(n_i, \tau_i)$ to $\mathcal{D}$, which is consulted during relation generation for type lookups.
70	The registry uses \emph{first-seen} semantics: when an entity name appears in multiple triples, the type assigned at its first occurrence governs all subsequent constraint checks, making type enforcement sensitive to generation order.
71	At each step $t$, the processor pattern-matches the decoded prefix to identify the current field position; semantic masks activate only at type-bearing positions (\textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}).
72	\label{sec:position-detection}
73	
74	\paragraph{Dynamic masking.}
75	\label{sec:dynamic-masking}
76	At type-bearing positions, the processor computes a semantic mask $S(t) \subseteq V$.
77	At a \textsc{HeadType} position, if $h_j \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}[h_j] \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)$, the mask allows only the registered type; otherwise it falls back to all domain-valid types $\operatorname{dom}(r_j)$.
78	At a \textsc{TailType} position, the mask restricts to $\operatorname{range}(r_j, \tau^h_j)$ conditioned on the already-determined head type, further narrowing to the registered type when $t_j \in \mathcal{D}$.
79	This sequential check achieves best-effort pair-based enforcement (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), strictly tighter than independent domain/range checking; ``best-effort'' reflects the grammar-first fallback (\S\ref{sec:composition}), which prioritizes JSON integrity over type validity when constraints conflict.
80	
81	\paragraph{Tokenizer-agnostic type masking.}
82	We use \emph{continuation masking} to handle context-dependent tokenizations and prefix-shared types (e.g., \textsc{Sen}/\textsc{Sid}/\textsc{Side} in WikiEvents): a compile-time prefix map identifies valid continuations for each type name, disambiguating over multiple steps across byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral).
83	
84	\paragraph{Grammar-semantic interaction.}
85	\label{sec:interaction}
86	The final mask is $G(t) \cap S(t)$; when empty, grammar-first fallback applies (\S\ref{sec:composition}), embodying this interaction: semantic constraints reduce DR by only 24\% without grammar-enforced vocabulary.
87	
88	
89	\subsection{Decoding Strategies}
90	\label{sec:strategies}
91	
92	\paragraph{S1 (joint extraction): Single-pass decoding.}
93	Both layers are active throughout generation; the entity registry populates during entity decoding and is immediately available for relation-level type checking.
94	
95	\paragraph{S2 (two-pass pipeline): Two-pass decoding.}\label{sec:s2}
96	A first pass extracts entities; these compile an input-dependent grammar for the second pass.
97	S1 achieves higher R-F1 at comparable DR (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}) and is the primary configuration.
98

1	% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion
2	
3	OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
4	The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
5	
6	\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
7	This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
8	We hypothesize this reflects improved vocabulary calibration: larger models assign higher probability to ontology-valid tokens, reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
9	Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
10	Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).
11	
12	\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
13	Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
14	Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
15	Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
16	Net effect: total violations decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and ${>}$90\% under fine-tuning; DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
17	
18	\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
19	GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
20	S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.
21	
22	\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
23	Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
24	Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We hypothesize this reflects improved vocabulary calibration: larger models assign higher probability to ontology-valid tokens, reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and ${>}$90\% under fine-tuning; DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We hypothesize this reflects improved vocabulary calibration: larger models assign higher probability to ontology-valid tokens, reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and ${>}$90\% under fine-tuning; DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.

% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Evaluated across three 8B-class models and two relation extraction datasets (up to 96 relations), OntoCoDec composed with LoRA fine-tuning reduces domain/range violations to near-zero ($\leq$\,0.21\%) at F1 40--46\%, but introduces cross-field type inconsistencies ($\leq$1.4\%) from per-triple enforcement.
Beam search ($k{=}2$) reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency; $k{=}4$ eliminates all violation types at 8B at 1.39$\times$.
In zero-shot settings, cross-field rates are higher (up to 12\%) but decrease with model calibration.
Zero-shot domain/range reductions span 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED; with scale- and schema-dependent layer interaction.
\end{abstract}

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) under both zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned settings, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework grounded in the observation that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We hypothesize this reflects improved vocabulary calibration: larger models assign higher probability to ontology-valid tokens, reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and ${>}$90\% under fine-tuning; DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 2 RE datasets (SciERC, DocRED) and 3 model families, with a preliminary event extraction pilot (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations (DR+CF) decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and 26--52\% under fine-tuned greedy S1; beam $k{=}4$ eliminates all. DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.

% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Evaluated across three 8B-class models and two relation extraction datasets (up to 96 relations), OntoCoDec composed with LoRA fine-tuning reduces domain/range violations to $\leq$\,0.21\% at F1 40--46\%, converting irrecoverable type errors to correctable cross-field inconsistencies (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 1.39$\times$ latency.
In zero-shot settings, DR reductions span 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED; CF increases are concentrated in hallucinated entities (58.1\%) and decrease with scale and fine-tuning.
\end{abstract}

1	% Appendix: Full Proof of Proposition 1
2	% Level 2 (prefix-decidable with state) constraints are not context-free.
3	
4	\section{Full Proof of Proposition 1}
5	\label{app:pumping-lemma}
6	
7	We prove that domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets cannot be expressed by any context-free grammar, using the pumping lemma for context-free languages.
8	
9	\begin{proof}
10	Define the language $L$ of valid IE outputs over ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ with $\mathcal{E} = \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, $\mathcal{R} = \{r\}$, and $\sigma(r) = \{(\tau_A, \tau_A)\}$ (i.e., $r$ requires both head and tail to be type $\tau_A$).
11	
12	An output string has the form:
13	\[
14	w = e_1\, e_2\, \cdots\, e_n\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_k,\, r,\, \tau^h)
15	\]
16	where each $e_i$ is an entity with type $\tau_{a_i} \in \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, and $\tau^h$ is the head type field of a relation triple referencing entity $e_k$ ($1 \leq k \leq n$).
17	
18	The type-validity constraint requires $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k}$ (the head type must match the referenced entity's type) \emph{and} $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau_A\}$.
19	Combined: a string $w \in L$ if and only if $\tau_{a_k} = \tau_A$.
20	
21	Now consider strings of the specific form:
22	\[
23	w_n = \underbrace{\tau_B\; \tau_B\; \cdots\; \tau_B}_{n-1}\; \tau_A\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_n,\, r,\, \tau_A)
24	\]
25	where the first $n{-}1$ entities have type $\tau_B$ and only entity $e_n$ has type $\tau_A$.
26	The relation references $e_n$, so $\tau^h = \tau_A = \tau_{a_n}$, satisfying both the registry consistency and domain constraint.
27	Thus $w_n \in L$ for all $n$.
28	
29	Assume for contradiction that $L$ is context-free.
30	By the pumping lemma, there exists a pumping length $p$ such that any $w \in L$ with $|w| \geq p$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ where:
31	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
32	    \item $|vy| \geq 1$,
33	    \item $|vxy| \leq p$,
34	    \item $uv^i xy^i z \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.
35	\end{enumerate}
36	
37	Choose $w = w_n$ with $n > p$.
38	The entity list portion $\tau_B^{n-1}\, \tau_A$ has length $n > p$, so the pumpable region $vxy$ (with $|vxy| \leq p$) must lie entirely within the entity list (it cannot span from the entity list to the relation reference, which is separated by $n - p > 0$ entity tokens from the start).
39	
40	\textbf{Case 1:} $v$ or $y$ contains entity tokens from the $\tau_B^{n-1}$ prefix.

% Appendix: Full Proof of Proposition 1
% Level 2 (prefix-decidable with state) constraints are not context-free.

\section{Full Proof of Proposition 1}
\label{app:pumping-lemma}

We prove that domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets cannot be expressed by any context-free grammar, using the pumping lemma for context-free languages.

\begin{proof}
Define the language $L$ of valid IE outputs over ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ with $\mathcal{E} = \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, $\mathcal{R} = \{r\}$, and $\sigma(r) = \{(\tau_A, \tau_A)\}$ (i.e., $r$ requires both head and tail to be type $\tau_A$).

An output string has the form:
\[
w = e_1\, e_2\, \cdots\, e_n\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_k,\, r,\, \tau^h)
\]
where each $e_i$ is an entity with type $\tau_{a_i} \in \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, and $\tau^h$ is the head type field of a relation triple referencing entity $e_k$ ($1 \leq k \leq n$).

The type-validity constraint requires $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k}$ (the head type must match the referenced entity's type) \emph{and} $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau_A\}$.
Combined: a string $w \in L$ if and only if $\tau_{a_k} = \tau_A$.

Now consider strings of the specific form:
\[
w_n = \underbrace{\tau_B\; \tau_B\; \cdots\; \tau_B}_{n-1}\; \tau_A\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_n,\, r,\, \tau_A)
\]
where the first $n{-}1$ entities have type $\tau_B$ and only entity $e_n$ has type $\tau_A$.
The relation references $e_n$, so $\tau^h = \tau_A = \tau_{a_n}$, satisfying both the registry consistency and domain constraint.
Thus $w_n \in L$ for all $n$.

Assume for contradiction that $L$ is context-free.
By the pumping lemma, there exists a pumping length $p$ such that any $w \in L$ with $|w| \geq p$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ where:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $|vy| \geq 1$,
    \item $|vxy| \leq p$,
    \item $uv^i xy^i z \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.
\end{enumerate}

Choose $w = w_n$ with $n > p$.
The entity list portion $\tau_B^{n-1}\, \tau_A$ has length $n > p$, so the pumpable region $vxy$ (with $|vxy| \leq p$) must lie entirely within the entity list (it cannot span from the entity list to the relation reference, which is separated by $n - p > 0$ entity tokens from the start).

\textbf{Case 1:} $v$ or $y$ contains entity tokens from the $\tau_B^{n-1}$ prefix.
Pumping up ($i = 2$): $uv^2 xy^2 z$ inserts additional $\tau_B$ entities, increasing $n$ to some $n' > n$.
But the relation reference still points to entity $e_n$ (at the original position), which is now at a different position in the longer entity list.
The entity at position $n$ in the pumped string is $\tau_B$ (since we inserted $\tau_B$ tokens before position $n$, shifting $\tau_A$ to position $n' > n$).
Thus $\tau^h = \tau_A \neq \tau_B = \tau_{a_n'}$, where $n'$ is the new position of entity $e_n$.
More precisely: the relation references a fixed entity name $e_k$, but pumping changes the entity-type binding at that name's position.
Since the pumped string assigns $\tau_B$ at position $k$ (which originally had $\tau_A$), the type-validity constraint $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k} \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$ is violated.
Hence $uv^2 xy^2 z \notin L$, contradicting condition (iii).

\textbf{Case 2:} $v$ or $y$ contains the $\tau_A$ token at position $n$.
Pumping down ($i = 0$): $uxz$ removes the only $\tau_A$ entity.
The relation's head entity reference now points to a position that either does not exist or has type $\tau_B$.
In either case, $\tau^h = \tau_A \neq \tau_B$, violating type validity.
Hence $uxz \notin L$, contradicting condition (iii).

In both cases, the pumping lemma is violated, so $L$ is not context-free.
The key insight is that type-validity requires a \emph{binding} between an entity's type (assigned at an earlier position) and the relation's type field (at a later position), with the binding target determined by the entity name.
Pumping disrupts this binding by changing which entity occupies a given position, while the relation reference remains fixed---a cross-position dependency that pushdown automata cannot track with their LIFO stack discipline.

OntoCoDec's semantic layer addresses this with a runtime entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ (a finite map), operating as a deterministic stateful transducer that provides random-access type lookups, beyond the expressive power of context-free grammars.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Finite entity sets.}
For a finite entity set $\mathcal{E}$ with canonical identifiers, the valid language $L_{\text{valid}} = \bigcap_i L_i$ is theoretically regular (a finite intersection of regular languages).
However, the corresponding DFA requires $O(|\mathcal{T}|^{|\mathcal{E}|})$ states---for SciERC with 6 entity types and typical documents containing 20+ entities, this exceeds $10^{15}$ states, rendering explicit construction impractical.
Moreover, real IE operates over open-vocabulary text spans rather than closed identifier sets, making the general (non-regular) formulation the appropriate model.
Proposition~1 motivates the runtime state-tracking architecture for this general case.

\paragraph{Position indexing vs.\ name referencing.}
The proof above uses position-based entity indexing ($e_k$ at position $k$) for expository clarity.
In OntoCoDec's actual JSON output, relation triples reference entities by name strings rather than positional indices.
Specifically, Case~1 of the pumping argument (position shift) does not directly apply under name-based referencing, since pumping does not change which entity a name refers to. However, the non-context-free conclusion still holds via a stronger argument:
validating type consistency requires a name$\to$type lookup over dynamically generated bindings, which is a random-access map operation.
A PDA's LIFO stack cannot perform random-access retrieval by key (it can only inspect the top element), so the non-context-free result holds regardless of whether entities are referenced by position or by name.
Name-based referencing strictly subsumes position-based indexing: any position-based constraint can be expressed via names (assign names $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ in order), but name-based constraints additionally permit cross-field coreference (the same entity name appearing in multiple triples must carry the same type), which position indexing cannot express.
Thus, the position-based formulation is a simplification that makes the pumping argument more transparent without weakening the conclusion.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) in zero-shot settings; Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B additionally under LoRA fine-tuning, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework grounded in the observation that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

68	\section*{Limitations}
69	
70	\paragraph{Constraint scope.}
71	CF is an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement: CF$\leftrightarrow$DR represents a fundamental trade-off (eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}), and its impact is model-dependent (S1 introduces CF for calibrated models but reduces it for poorly-calibrated ones).
72	Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF.
73	Entity-first generation order is an architectural constraint: the grammar enforces entities before relations, ensuring the registry is populated before type checks; alternative orderings would require deferred constraint evaluation.
74	Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations total) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors (28\%); schema gaps arise from training-data-derived constraints that may not cover all valid type pairs (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
75	Our empirical constraints are derived from training data type-pair co-occurrences; schema evolution (adding new entity types or relations) would require constraint regeneration, and the 0.6--1.0\% uncovered valid type pairs suggest potential over-restriction during transition periods.
76	We do not decompose CF violations into first-seen cascading errors versus legitimate type ambiguity; this decomposition requires gold entity type annotations at the mention level, which SciERC provides only at the entity level.
77	Post-hoc type consensus re-voting eliminates all CF in our experiments, at the cost of DR regression (up to $+$9.38\,pp on DocRED zero-shot; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}); integrating consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.
78	
79	\paragraph{Evaluation coverage.}
80	Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated on two 8B-class models (full datasets) and one 70B-class model (SciERC full, DocRED 200-document subset).
81	Scaling to smaller models has not been verified; the schema restrictiveness--enforcement difficulty relationship is based on three schemas.
82	Evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); LoRA hyperparameters were tuned on SciERC and transferred to DocRED without dataset-specific optimization, which may underestimate DocRED potential.
83	WikiEvents fine-tuning is preliminary ($n{=}20$); DocRED uses the development set (test annotations unavailable).
84	All main experiments use greedy decoding; beam search compatibility is confirmed but comprehensive evaluation across all configurations remains future work (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling},~\ref{app:beam-search}).
85	
86	\paragraph{Engineering considerations.}
87	Our approach requires access to model logits, excluding API-only models; continuation masking assumes distinguishable token prefixes per type name, which may be challenged by morphologically similar types (e.g., \texttt{Protein} vs.\ \texttt{Protein\_Complex}; Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).
88	70B experiments use AWQ INT4 quantization; an 8B ablation confirms enforcement is unaffected (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}), though a direct 70B FP16 comparison exceeds our hardware capacity.

% === Limitations (ARR requirement: standalone section, does not count toward page limit) ===
\clearpage
\section*{Limitations}

\paragraph{Constraint scope.}
CF is an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement: CF$\leftrightarrow$DR represents a fundamental trade-off (eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}), and its impact is model-dependent (S1 introduces CF for calibrated models but reduces it for poorly-calibrated ones).
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF.
Entity-first generation order is an architectural constraint: the grammar enforces entities before relations, ensuring the registry is populated before type checks; alternative orderings would require deferred constraint evaluation.
Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations total) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors (28\%); schema gaps arise from training-data-derived constraints that may not cover all valid type pairs (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
Our empirical constraints are derived from training data type-pair co-occurrences; schema evolution (adding new entity types or relations) would require constraint regeneration, and the 0.6--1.0\% uncovered valid type pairs suggest potential over-restriction during transition periods.
We do not decompose CF violations into first-seen cascading errors versus legitimate type ambiguity; this decomposition requires gold entity type annotations at the mention level, which SciERC provides only at the entity level.
Post-hoc type consensus re-voting eliminates all CF in our experiments, at the cost of DR regression (up to $+$9.38\,pp on DocRED zero-shot; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}); integrating consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.

\paragraph{Evaluation coverage.}
Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated on two 8B-class models (full datasets) and one 70B-class model (SciERC full, DocRED 200-document subset).
Scaling to smaller models has not been verified; the schema restrictiveness--enforcement difficulty relationship is based on three schemas.
Evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); LoRA hyperparameters were tuned on SciERC and transferred to DocRED without dataset-specific optimization, which may underestimate DocRED potential.
WikiEvents fine-tuning is preliminary ($n{=}20$); DocRED uses the development set (test annotations unavailable).
All main experiments use greedy decoding; beam search compatibility is confirmed but comprehensive evaluation across all configurations remains future work (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling},~\ref{app:beam-search}).

\paragraph{Engineering considerations.}
Our approach requires access to model logits, excluding API-only models; continuation masking assumes distinguishable token prefixes per type name, which may be challenged by morphologically similar types (e.g., \texttt{Protein} vs.\ \texttt{Protein\_Complex}; Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).
70B experiments use AWQ INT4 quantization; an 8B ablation confirms enforcement is unaffected (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}), though a direct 70B FP16 comparison exceeds our hardware capacity.
Evaluation is limited to English-language datasets; the mechanism is language-independent but CJK tokenization fragmentation may increase masking steps (Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).
While composability is validated with both LoRA and full fine-tuning (Appendix~\ref{app:full-ft}), different PEFT methods may affect logit distributions differently, and further validation across adapter methods is warranted.
The two-pass strategy (S2) exhibits scale-dependent degradation: at 70B, S2 reduces R-F1 by 8.45\,pp while 8B models show comparable S1/S2 performance, suggesting optimal constraint granularity varies with model capacity (Appendix~\ref{app:70b-ablation}).
